page.title: One Language for Every Tree
page.description: Fetch JSON from the web, select the bits you care about, and print or save the result — one tree selection language for everything

content.p: Here's the big idea: you only have to learn one tree/table selection language for absolutely everything. JSON from a website. XML on disk. A directory tree. A parse tree (RakuAST or Match). CSV, SQL, and other tabular forms. Same axes, same operators, same mental model.

That language currently lives in Qwiratry — a Raku architecture for declarative queries and flexible data walking. The longer-term goal is that the core of Qwiratry be integrated into Raku itself; the reason is that we need tree-handling capabilities to make Macros possible. This article is the first in a series aimed at presenting Qwiratry to the Raku community. The plan is that this first sub-series will start with basic Tree Transformation, and we'll then go on to cover other topics like:

ul.li: Extending Qwiratry trees to handle other data formats

content.p: All of these will hopefully be shown by doing useful things rather than by reading a specification.
Qwiratry is still young (0.0.x), so it will evolve somewhat as it goes on. The concepts, however, should remain.
By the end of this tutorial you should be able to:

ul.li: Read JSON from the internet (or a file)
Select parts of it with navigation operators
Render results (and optionally write them somewhere)
Combine data from more than one query on related sources

content.p: The worked example at the end is: take a list of modules from the ecosystem, read each source-url, and for GitHub repos fetch how many contributors they have — then print a small JSON report.
You'll need RakuAST enabled, the core module, and a couple of plugins:
content.code: export RAKUDO_RAKUAST=1 zef install Qwiratry Qwiratry::Format::JSON Qwiratry::Location::HTTP
content.p: In your script, load the query slang so the Unicode operators are available:
content.h1: The Pipeline: Source → Parse → Query → Render → Destination
content.p: If you prefer English names instead of unicode operators, the slang also provides aliases such as child, descendant, and attribute for the main navigation operators.
Almost every useful tree job has the same shape:

tr.td: Read bytes/text from a file, URL, or similar location
Turn text into a walkable tree (JSON, XML, …)
Walk the tree and keep what you want
Serialise a tree back to text
Write the result somewhere (file, HTTP POST, …)

content.p: Not all of those parts are necessary. For example, if you want to display the data, you probably won't use the Destination operator (but you may use Render to put it into a human-readable table).

Read that left to right: fetch the URL, parse as JSON, find descendant item nodes, keep those whose price attribute is greater than 100, and print pretty JSON. Swap the final say … ↴ for … ↴ <JSON> ⮷ <expensive-items.json> when you do want a file.
GitHub's public API is a friendly playground. Let's pull one repository's JSON and keep a few fields:

⥷ is the attribute operator: on a JSON object it reads a key's value. ⪪ (child) follows into nested objects or arrays; ⪪⪪ (descendant) walks all the way down. For a GitHub repo payload, $repo ⪪ <owner> yields the nested owner object, and $repo ⪪⪪ <login> finds the owner's login wherever it sits under the root.
You can also select and print in one expression when the selection itself is the payload you want:
content.code: # Keep only the owner object, print it say ($repo ⪪ <owner>) ↴ <JSON> :pretty;
content.h1: More Than One Query on Related Sources
content.p: Often you want two slices from the same neighbourhood of the web, then combine them. Union (∪) is the blunt instrument — useful when both sides are lists of the same kind of node:

When the rows share keys and you want a relational join, Qwiratry also has join operators such as ⨝ (inner / natural join) and ≜ (natural join alias). The next tutorial in this series leans on those more deliberately (JSON from the web joined with YAML from disk). For the ecosystem example below, a little Raku glue to build report rows is clearer than forcing a join before you've seen mixed sources properly.

What this shows off:

ul.li: Source + parse for each contributors URL
Attribute navigation on both remote JSON and local meta hashes
Render (to stdout here — add ⮷ if you want a file)
A realistic mix of Qwiratry pipelines and a little Raku for URL shaping and looping — Tree Transformation is a tool, not a religion
